title: Association of Race and Socioeconomic Status with Hemodialysis Arteriovenous Access Outcomes.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Arteriovenous access is essential for long-term hemodialysis. The creation and maintenance of arteriovenous fistula (AVF) or arteriovenous graft (AVG) are critical for effective dialysis and minimizing complications. However, the influence of race and social determinants of health on presentation, management, and outcomes has not been well evaluated. This study uses the Vascular Quality Initiative (VQI) database to evaluate disparities in vascular access outcomes by race and community-level disadvantage. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective study using the VQI database to identify adults who underwent AVF or AVG creation for hemodialysis between 2016 and 2023. The Area Deprivation Index (ADI), a validated measure of neighborhood socioeconomic disadvantage incorporating income, education, employment, and housing quality, was categorized into quartiles from least (Q1) to most disadvantaged (Q4). Patients without follow-up data, recorded complications, or ADI information were excluded. Predisposing factors and postoperative outcomes considering race and ADI were analyzed. Group comparisons were performed using chi-squared tests and t-tests. Multivariable logistic regression adjusted for demographic and clinical covariates was used to assess associations. All analyses were conducted using IBM SPSS Statistics version 30 (IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). RESULTS: A total of 77,544 patients were included (mean age 62.2 years, 43.4% female). White patients represented the largest racial group (51.5%, n = 39,959), and 29.5% (n = 22,850) were from the most disadvantaged ADI quartile. AVF maturation was more delayed in White versus Black patients (adjusted OR 1.43, 95% CI: 1.21-1.70, P < 0.001). Immediate postoperative bleeding was less common in White versus Black patients (0.6% vs. 0.9%; OR 0.58,0.43-0.79, P < 0.001) and less frequent in Q4 versus Q1 (0.5% vs. 1.2%; OR 0.36, 0.25-0.53, P < 0.001). At 9 months, access patency was lower in Black versus White patients (86.4% vs. 88.2%, P = 0.003) and varied by ADI (P < 0.001), with Q1 achieving the highest patency (88.7%). Nine-month mortality was highest in White patients (28% vs. 21% in Black, P < 0.001 unadjusted); however, only Asian race remained independently protective after adjustment (OR 0.41, 0.35-0.47, P < 0.001 vs. Black). Patients in Q4 had significantly higher 9-month mortality compared to Q1 (adjusted OR 1.56, 1.46-1.67, P < 0.001). CONCLUSION: Significant disparities in hemodialysis access outcomes exist by race and socioeconomic status. Patients in disadvantaged areas experienced higher rates of maturation delay and mortality. Black and American Indian/Alaskan Native patients had worse patency and greater AVG use. Structural and social factors strongly influence vascular access outcomes, underscoring the need for targeted interventions to improve equity in hemodialysis care.

The creation and maintenance of arteriovenous fistula (AVF) or arteriovenous graft (AVG) are critical for effective dialysis and minimizing complications. However, the influence of race and social determinants of health on presentation, management, and outcomes has not been well evaluated.

title: Intraosseous venous malformation of the distal fibula treated with image-guided sclerotherapy and embolization.
abstract: n Intraosseous venous malformations are rare slow-flow vascular lesions in which involvement of lower-extremity long bones is uncommon. A 51-year-old woman with antithrombin III deficiency and post-thrombotic syndrome presented with focal left leg pain initially attributed to chronic venous disease. Computed tomography venography demonstrated a serpiginous intraosseous lesion within the distal fibula communicating with the peroneal venous system. Image-guided selective embolization was performed using foam sclerotherapy and-butyl cyanoacrylate. Postprocedural imaging confirmed exclusion of the lesion. At follow-up, the patient reported resolution of focal bone pain without radiographic recurrence. This case illustrates diagnostic considerations and technical management of symptomatic lower-extremity intraosseous venous malformations.

title: Antiphospholipid syndrome: epidemiology and outcomes in the evolving criteria era.
abstract: Antiphospholipid syndrome (APS) is a heterogeneous autoimmune thrombo-inflammatory disorder characterized by thrombosis, pregnancy morbidity and an expanding spectrum of microvascular, cardiac, haematological and other systemic manifestations. Although research has provided considerable insights into the pathogenesis and clinical phenotypes of APS, its epidemiology remains difficult to define because estimates depend on case definitions, antibody testing, repeat-testing requirements, testing practices and data sources. Population-based studies suggest that APS is rare, and catastrophic APS is rarer and best understood through registry data. Antiphospholipid antibody positivity alone does not establish APS; transient or low-level positivity can occur without disease, whereas persistent antibodies must be interpreted alongside compatible clinical manifestations. Despite its rarity, APS causes substantial morbidity through recurrent thrombosis, organ damage and adverse pregnancy outcomes, supporting targeted evaluation in unprovoked or recurrent venous thromboembolism, stroke in younger adults and selected pregnancy complications. Apparent differences among populations can reflect ascertainment, access to testing, study design and biological variation. Standardized case definitions, antibody testing and laboratory reporting, together with longitudinal population-based research in ancestry-diverse, paediatric and low-income and middle-income populations, are needed to refine estimates of APS burden and define its clinical spectrum.

Although research has provided considerable insights into the pathogenesis and clinical phenotypes of APS, its epidemiology remains difficult to define because estimates depend on case definitions, antibody testing, repeat-testing requirements, testing practices and data sources. Population-based studies suggest that APS is rare, and catastrophic APS is rarer and best understood through registry data.

title: Contemporary Outcomes of Isolated Common Femoral Endarterectomy in the Endovascular Era.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Common femoral endarterectomy (CFE) remains the reference treatment for common femoral artery (CFA) occlusive disease, yet contemporary real-world data focused specifically on isolated CFE remain limited. This study aimed to evaluate the clinical profile, operative characteristics, and outcomes of isolated CFE performed in a tertiary vascular surgery center, with particular emphasis on postoperative complications, reintervention and occlusion, as well as the possible influence of wound closure technique and hemostatic adjunct use on local morbidity. METHODS: A retrospective observational study was conducted including consecutive patients who underwent isolated CFE between January 2013 and December 2023. Baseline characteristics, clinical presentation, lesion complexity, operative details, postoperative complications, reinterventions, and postoperative occlusion were analyzed. Lesions were classified according to Trans-Atlantic Inter-Society Consensus II (TASC II). Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to assess freedom from occlusion, while Cox regression was performed to explore factors associated with postoperative occlusion. Fisher's exact test was used to assess associations between wound closure technique, hemostatic adjunct use, and postoperative complications. RESULTS: A total of 96 patients underwent 100 isolated CFEs. The mean age was 68.5 ± 9 years, 89% were male, and 63% presented with chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI). Most lesions were classified as TASC A-B (68%). The median follow up was 3.5 years (95% confidence interval [CI], 3.2-3.9). Early postoperative complications were predominantly local, including groin hematoma (4%), lymphatic leakage (4%), lymphocele (5%), pseudoaneurysm (2%), and infection (8%). Overall, 18% of procedures required reintervention, with 14% undergoing open and 4% endovascular reintervention. Nine occlusive events occurred during follow up. Estimated freedom from occlusion was 100% at 30 days, 96% at 1 year, and 86% at 5 years. TASC C-D lesions showed a numerically higher occlusion rate than TASC A-B lesions (12.5% vs. 7.4%; OR, 1.80), although this difference was not statistically significant (P = 0.462). In univariable Cox regression, aspirin therapy was the only variable significantly associated with lower risk of postoperative occlusion (hazard ratio [HR], 0.20; P = 0.026). Neither intradermal wound closure nor hemostatic adjunct use was significantly associated with postoperative complications. CONCLUSION: Isolated CFE remains a safe and durable treatment for CFA occlusive disease, with low rates of early local complications, acceptable reintervention rates and good freedom from occlusion during follow up. These findings support the continued role of isolated CFE as the reference treatment for CFA disease in the endovascular era.

title: Cumulative operative burden is associated with poorer function after segmental bone transport for lower-extremity long-bone defects.
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Segmental bone transport offers biological reconstruction and limb preservation for extensive lower-extremity long-bone defects, but treatment often involves prolonged external fixation, planned stages, and unplanned reoperations. We evaluated reconstructive and functional outcomes and examined the association between cumulative operative burden and final patient-reported function. METHODS: This retrospective single-centre study screened 44 patients treated between January 2012 and March 2023. Thirty-six patients, representing 37 reconstructed long bones, had complete final outcome ascertainment. ASAMI bone outcome was reported per reconstructed bone (n = 37); limb preservation and all functional and multivariable analyses were patient-level (n = 36). Outcomes included limb preservation, ASAMI bone and functional results, the Lower Extremity Functional Scale (LEFS), the Karlström-Olerud score, healing indices, treatment-related events, and the cumulative number of formal operations. Multivariable linear regression, bootstrap resampling, sensitivity analyses, and exploratory receiver operating characteristic analysis were performed. RESULTS: Mean defect length was 10.32 ± 4.67 cm and the mean defect-to-bone length ratio was 26.3% ± 12.4%. Patients underwent a mean of 8.08 ± 4.21 operations (median, 7; range, 3-18). Mean follow-up after external-fixator removal was 5.69 ± 3.62 years. Limb preservation was achieved in 35 of 36 patients (97.2%). Combined excellent/good ASAMI bone and functional outcomes were 75.7% and 77.8%, respectively. Pin-site infection occurred in 17 patients and accounted for 32 fixation-element events; premature consolidation occurred in 11 patients and accounted for 18 episodes. After adjustment for age, defect length, and consolidation index, each additional operation was associated with a 1.94-point lower LEFS (β=-1.94, 95% CI - 3.12 to - 0.76; p=.002). Excluding the patient who underwent below-knee amputation and had an LEFS of 0 did not materially alter this association (n = 35; β=-1.86, 95% CI - 2.85 to - 0.86; p<.001). Older age was also independently associated with lower LEFS (β=-0.46 points/year; p=.006). Follow-up duration was not associated with LEFS and did not alter the principal association. Exploratory ROC analysis for LEFS < 40 yielded an AUC of 0.846 (bootstrap 95% CI 0.689-0.968); the internally derived ≥ 11-operation threshold was regarded as hypothesis-generating. CONCLUSION: Segmental bone transport achieved high limb preservation and largely favourable ASAMI outcomes despite a substantial treatment burden. A greater cumulative number of operations was associated with lower final LEFS. Operation count should be interpreted as a summary marker of case complexity and the treatment course, not as evidence that repeated surgery alone caused poorer function.

We evaluated reconstructive and functional outcomes and examined the association between cumulative operative burden and final patient-reported function. METHODS: This retrospective single-centre study screened 44 patients treated between January 2012 and March 2023.

title: Retained Guidewire Following Perforator Vein Ablation.
abstract: Wire embolization is a rare but potentially serious complication of endovascular procedures. Endovenous thermal ablation is a minimally invasive procedure widely used to treat chronic venous insufficiency. Herein, we report a case of guidewire embolization into the posterior tibial and popliteal veins during endovenous laser ablation treatment that was successfully managed with open surgical retrieval. Because of the extensive length and location of the retained guidewire, inability to obtain reliable distal venous access, and concern for further migration or venous injury with percutaneous manipulation, open surgical retrieval was selected. The guidewire was successfully removed through popliteal vein exploration without perioperative complications. This case highlights the importance of recognizing retained intravascular foreign bodies promptly and maintaining open surgical retrieval as an option when endovascular techniques increase procedural risk.

title: A Giant Atherosclerotic Ascending Aortic Aneurysm (13.5 cm) With Arch Involvement Successfully Managed by Valve-Sparing Total Arch Replacement: A Case Report.
abstract: Giant ascending aortic aneurysms (AscAAs), conventionally defined as aneurysms exceeding 10 cm in diameter, are exceedingly rare in contemporary practice due to earlier diagnosis and prophylactic surgical intervention. AscAAs of atherosclerotic origin are particularly uncommon because proximal thoracic aortic aneurysms are typically associated with medial degeneration, connective tissue disorders, or bicuspid aortic valve disease rather than advanced atherosclerosis. Reports of aneurysms exceeding 13 cm remain exceptional in the literature. We report the case of a 70-year-old woman with multiple cardiovascular risk factors, including heavy tobacco exposure and type 2 diabetes mellitus, who presented with progressive dyspnea, constitutional symptoms, and hemodynamic compromise. Computed tomography angiography demonstrated a giant AscAA measuring 13.5 cm with extension into the aortic arch (8.7 cm), associated with periaortic fluid and imaging features suggestive of impending rupture. The aortic root and descending thoracic aorta were spared. Emergency open surgical repair was successfully performed using supracoronary ascending aortic replacement, total arch replacement under deep hypothermic circulatory arrest, and separate supra-aortic branch reconstruction with a branched Dacron graft. Histopathology confirmed an atheromatous aneurysm with thrombotic degeneration, while microbiological studies excluded infection. This case highlights the extreme rarity of massive atherosclerotic AscAAs and demonstrates that successful treatment is achievable through advanced, anatomy-driven open surgical reconstruction. Complete valve-sparing total arch replacement with separate branch vessel reconstruction provided durable exclusion of extensive disease while preserving native root structures. This report adds to the limited literature on extreme-diameter ascending aneurysms and underscores the importance of prompt diagnosis and individualized operative planning.

AscAAs of atherosclerotic origin are particularly uncommon because proximal thoracic aortic aneurysms are typically associated with medial degeneration, connective tissue disorders, or bicuspid aortic valve disease rather than advanced atherosclerosis. Reports of aneurysms exceeding 13 cm remain exceptional in the literature.

title: Herpes zoster as a trigger of cardiovascular events: A systematic review of epidemiological evidence and pathophysiological mechanisms.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Herpes zoster (HZ) has been associated with acute cardiovascular and cerebrovascular events, particularly stroke. We systematically reviewed epidemiological evidence and biological mechanisms linking HZ to vascular outcomes. METHODS: PubMed/MEDLINE, Scopus, Web of Science, and Embase were searched for observational studies evaluating cardiovascular or cerebrovascular events after HZ or herpes zoster ophthalmicus (HZO). Cohort, case-control, self-controlled case-series, and case-crossover studies were eligible. Mechanistic reports were considered separately to assess biological plausibility. RESULTS: Of 594 records identified, 204 were screened, 11 full-text reports were assessed, and 5 epidemiological studies were included in the primary synthesis. Stroke showed the most consistent association with HZ. Risk was greatest during the first weeks and months after infection, with self-controlled analyses indicating a peak approximately 3-4 weeks after HZ onset. HZO was associated with greater cerebrovascular risk than general HZ. Evidence for myocardial infarction and peripheral arterial disease was suggestive but less consistent. Mechanistic evidence supported roles for varicella-zoster virus-associated vasculopathy, inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, thrombosis, vascular remodeling, and plaque destabilization. CONCLUSIONS: Clinically manifest HZ is associated with a transient increase in vascular risk, most consistently for stroke. The temporal pattern and stronger association after HZO support HZ as a potential acute vascular trigger, while evidence for myocardial infarction and other vascular outcomes remains less robust.

title: Use of smart glasses for ultrasound-guided central venous catheterization in adults: a randomized clinical trial.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Head-mounted displays can be integrated with ultrasonography to overlay the image in the operator's field of view, improving hand-eye coordination during invasive procedures. The clinical efficacy of smart glasses for central venous catheterization (CVC) remains uncertain. This study aimed to evaluate whether using smart glasses can improve efficiency compared to conventional ultrasound-guided CVC. METHODS: This prospective, single-blinded, controlled study enrolled adult patients who underwent elective surgery requiring CVC. Patients were assigned to either the ultrasound screen (control) or smart glasses group using stratified randomization according to operator qualification. The primary outcome was the overall CVC procedural time. Secondary outcomes included ultrasound scanning and venous access time, number of needle redirections and probe repositionings, procedural success and complication rates. RESULTS: In total, 124 patients were analyzed. The overall procedural time was significantly reduced in the smart glasses group compared to that in the control group (158 [140, 189] s vs. 134 [117,150] s; median difference, 26.0 s; 95% CI, [16.0-37.0] s, P < 0.001). Specifically, the ultrasound scanning time (median difference, 3.0 s, P = 0.004), venous access time (median difference, 2.0 s, P = 0.013), number of needle redirections (median difference, 1.0, P = 0.003) and probe repositionings (median difference, 0.0, P = 0.005) were significantly reduced in the smart glasses group compared to those in the control group. However, the success and complication rates were comparable between groups. CONCLUSIONS: Smart glasses modestly improved procedural efficiency in ultrasound-guided CVC, potientially for novices, without improving success or complication rates. Larger-sample studies with more diverse operators and patients are warranted. title: Endovascular Management With a Fenestration Technique of an Iatrogenic Thoracic Chronic Type B Aortic Dissection.
abstract: We report the case of an 86-year-old woman who developed an intraoperative type B aortic dissection during ascending aortic replacement for an ascending aortic aneurysm. Postoperative imaging demonstrated an uncomplicated dissection extending to the infrarenal aorta. At 10 weeks, follow-up imaging revealed rapid aneurysmal expansion of the false lumen. Thoracic endovascular aortic repair was performed with adjunctive cerebrospinal fluid drainage, rapid pacing, and image fusion guidance. An intimal fenestration technique was used to optimize the distal sealing zone, extending the disruption from a pre-existing re-entry tear. A type Ib endoleak necessitated additional stent-graft deployment, which in turn caused occlusion of the left renal and superior mesenteric arteries. The STABILISE technique (stent-assisted balloon-induced intimal disruption and relamination in aortic dissection repair) with a PETTICOAT (Provisional Extension To Induce Complete Attachment) bare stent restored renal perfusion, and targeted stenting re-established mesenteric flow. A postprocedural pseudoaneurysm was managed conservatively and resolved with spontaneous thrombosis within 48 hours. The patient was discharged on postoperative day seven, asymptomatic, with complete exclusion of the dissection, patent visceral vessels, and no endoleak confirmed at six-week follow-up. This case illustrates that combining distal flap fenestration with STABILISE relamination and a comprehensive endovascular toolkit can successfully manage complex chronic type B aortic dissections, even in elderly, high-risk patients-provided that adequate perioperative safety measures and a broad endovascular armamentarium are available to address unanticipated complications.

Postoperative imaging demonstrated an uncomplicated dissection extending to the infrarenal aorta. At 10 weeks, follow-up imaging revealed rapid aneurysmal expansion of the false lumen.

title: Atheroembolic Blue Toe Syndrome Progressing to Below-Knee Amputation Despite Attempted Source Control and Revascularization: A Case Report.
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa Staphylococcus aureus Blue toe syndrome is characterized by painful blue or violaceous discoloration of one or more toes caused by impaired digital arterial perfusion. We present a 72-year-old woman with peripheral arterial disease, diabetes mellitus, antiphospholipid syndrome, and prior thromboembolic disease who developed dusky-blue discoloration of the left third toe. Initial arterial duplex demonstrated no major arterial occlusion, while computed tomography angiography with runoff showed distal infrarenal aortic soft plaque and distal tibial/pedal arterial disease. The aortic lesion was considered the suspected proximal embolic source in the setting of concomitant distal tibial and pedal arterial disease. The patient underwent endovascular aortic repair for proximal source control, but the left third toe nevertheless progressed to dry gangrene and required amputation. Over the following months, she developed nonhealing wounds, infections withand methicillin-resistant(MRSA), worsened distal perfusion, and osteomyelitis. There were multiple limb salvage procedures, including angioplasty, toe amputation, common plantar embolectomy, plantar bypass, transmetatarsal amputation, Achilles tendon lengthening, antibiotic bead placement, and external fixation. Following these procedures, however, the foot developed worsening ischemic and infected tissue loss and needed an emergency left below-knee amputation. Final pathology demonstrated significant findings, including gangrenous necrosis, chronic osteomyelitis, calcific atherosclerosis, and tibial vessel occlusions. This case showcases how blue toe syndrome can progress despite source control when severe distal runoff disease, poor wound oxygenation, and recurrent infections are present.

title: Detection of serum amyloid A in Saliva of patients with internal carotid artery stenosis: a pilot study.
abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine whether serum amyloid A (SAA) is detectable in saliva of patients with internal carotid artery (ICA) stenosis and to investigate the relationship between salivary and serum SAA levels across the perioperative period of carotid endarterectomy (CEA). MATERIALS AND METHODS: Six patients with asymptomatic ICA stenosis (60-99%) undergoing CEA were enrolled. Periodontal status was assessed at enrolment and used to characterise the cohort and document potential oral inflammatory confounding of salivary SAA. Salivary and serum SAA, C-reactive protein (CRP), and lipid parameters were measured before CEA, on postoperative day 2, and 30-45 days postoperatively using enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) and standard laboratory methods. RESULTS: SAA was detectable in all saliva samples. Serum SAA increased after surgery and did not decline at follow-up, whereas salivary SAA showed a progressive decline (repeated measures ANOVA: F(2,4) = 25.01, p = 0.005). A strong negative correlation was observed between changes in serum and salivary SAA (Pearson's r = - 0.976, p = 0.004). CONCLUSIONS: In this small pilot cohort, SAA was detectable in all saliva samples, and salivary concentrations decreased across the perioperative time points while serum SAA did not show a parallel decline. The observed inverse serum-saliva association should be interpreted cautiously given the very small sample size, absence of a control group, and potential oral and sampling confounders. These findings support the feasibility of measuring salivary SAA in this clinical setting and warrant confirmation in larger controlled studies.

title: Paget-Schroetter Syndrome With Focal Subclavian Arterial Stenosis Following Repetitive Overhead Activity: A Case Report.
abstract: Paget-Schroetter syndrome (PSS), also known as effort thrombosis, is a rare form of upper extremity deep vein thrombosis resulting from mechanical compression of the subclavian vein at the thoracic outlet. It typically occurs in young, active individuals performing strenuous upper limb exercises and presents with pain, swelling, and discoloration of the affected limb. Early diagnosis and specialist management are important for optimizing outcomes. In selected patients, management may include a combined endovascular and surgical approach to restore venous patency and reduce the risk of recurrence and post-thrombotic complications. A 46-year-old woman who was neither an athlete nor a manual laborer presented with a four-day history of right upper-limb pain and swelling following repetitive overhead activity. She reported progressive swelling, positional bluish discoloration on arm elevation, and episodic pallor of the thumb and index finger. No secondary provoking factor for venous thromboembolism was identified. Physical examination revealed a swollen right arm with prominent superficial veins and bluish discoloration provoked within 10-15 seconds of arm elevation. Initial duplex ultrasonography identified right subclavian vein thrombosis, with the axillary and brachial veins reported as patent. However, computed tomography (CT) venography performed the following day demonstrated thrombosis involving both the right axillary and subclavian veins. CT angiography additionally demonstrated focal stenosis of the right subclavian artery at the thoracic outlet. The patient underwent catheter-directed thrombolysis followed by first rib resection for thoracic outlet decompression. This case documents PSS outside its typical demographic in a patient presenting with upper limb swelling and discoloration following repetitive overhead activity. The discordant axillary vein findings emphasize the importance of interpreting sequential vascular imaging studies in the context of their timing and modality. The accompanying episodic digital pallor and CT finding of focal subclavian arterial stenosis highlight the importance of considering possible arterial involvement in a predominantly venous presentation. Following treatment, the symptoms resolved, and venous patency was maintained at four-week follow-up.
englishSummary: Paget-Schroetter syndrome (PSS), also known as effort thrombosis, is a rare form of upper extremity deep vein thrombosis resulting from mechanical compression of the subclavian vein at the thoracic outlet. It typically occurs in young, active individuals performing strenuous upper limb exercises and presents with pain, swelling, and discoloration of the affected limb. Early diagnosis and specialist management are important for optimizing outcomes.

title: Venous Thromboembolism Prophylaxis in Hospitalized Medical Patients: A Narrative Review of Risk Stratification, Treatment Duration, and Bleeding Trade-Offs.
abstract: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains a leading preventable cause of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized medical patients, yet decisions about who should receive prophylaxis - and for how long - remain far from settled. This review synthesizes evidence from 22 sources, including randomized trials, prospective and retrospective cohorts, systematic reviews, and major society guidelines, addressing risk stratification, in-hospital anticoagulant prophylaxis, extended-duration direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), the associated bleeding trade-offs, and real-world implementation. The evidence broadly supports pharmacologic prophylaxis during hospitalization for appropriately selected, acutely ill medical patients with acceptable bleeding risk, with the strongest randomized evidence favoring low-molecular-weight heparin during the inpatient period. That benefit comes with trade-offs worth weighing carefully, since even well-supported regimens carry a measurable increase in bleeding risk alongside their protective effect. Commonly used risk-assessment tools have real limitations as well: the Padua and IMPROVE scores offer a useful clinical framework, but head-to-head comparison shows both discriminate poorly between patients who will and won't develop VTE, and real-world implementation data reveal frequent misclassification and inconsistent dose administration. Extended-duration anticoagulation after discharge follows a similar pattern across the major DOAC trials in this space - fewer thrombotic events, but more bleeding, without a clear survival benefit. Taken together, this evidence points toward a risk-adapted rather than protocol-driven approach: assess VTE and bleeding risk at admission, initiate appropriate inpatient prophylaxis, reassess as the clinical picture changes, confirm that prescribed doses are actually being given, and reserve extended anticoagulation after discharge for carefully selected patients rather than applying it as a default. Meaningful progress in this area will likely come less from another static risk score and more from models that can track mobility, bleeding risk, and treatment response dynamically over the course of a hospital stay.
englishSummary: Venous thromboembolism (VTE) remains a leading preventable cause of morbidity and mortality in hospitalized medical patients, yet decisions about who should receive prophylaxis - and for how long - remain far from settled. This review synthesizes evidence from 22 sources, including randomized trials, prospective and retrospective cohorts, systematic reviews, and major society guidelines, addressing risk stratification, in-hospital anticoagulant prophylaxis, extended-duration direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs), the associated bleeding trade-offs, and real-world implementation. The evidence broadly supports pharmacologic prophylaxis during hospitalization for appropriately selected, acutely ill medical patients with acceptable bleeding risk, with the strongest randomized evidence favoring low-molecular-weight heparin during the inpatient period.

title: Mechanical Thrombectomy for Pulmonary Tumor Embolism Masquerading as Bland Pulmonary Embolism: A Case Report.
abstract: Pulmonary tumor embolism (PTE) is a rare but potentially life-threatening form of non-thrombotic pulmonary embolism. Despite advancements in management, it remains a challenging entity due to its unpredictable clinical course and high mortality rate. With the advent of minimally invasive endovascular treatment modalities, the management of pulmonary embolism has witnessed a shift from systemic thrombolysis or surgical thromboarterectomy to catheter-directed thrombolysis, mechanical thrombectomy, or pharmaco-mechanical thrombectomy, combining mechanical thrombectomy with catheter-directed thrombolysis. We report a rare case of intermediate-risk pulmonary tumor embolism managed by large-bore aspiration thrombectomy.

title: Interventional Management of Patients with Hepatocellular Carcinoma and Portal Vein Tumor Thrombosis: Are There Differences Between East and West?
abstract: PURPOSE OF REVIEW: This review summarizes current evidence on interventional therapies for hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) with portal vein tumor thrombosis (PVTT), compares the treatment strategies between East and West, and proposes a practical framework for patient selection in the immunotherapy era of HCC. RECENT FINDINGS: Although systemic therapy remains the primary treatment for advanced HCC with PVTT, selected interventional therapies may provide additional value in carefully chosen patients with preserved liver function, liver-dominant disease, anatomically targetable PVTT, and adequate or reconstructable portal venous flow. Interventional options include transarterial chemoembolization, hepatic arterial infusion chemotherapy, transarterial radioembolization/selective internal radiation therapy, radiotherapy, portal vein stenting, and iodine-125 seed-based endovascular brachytherapy. Eastern and Western practice patterns differ mainly in the threshold for locoregional intensification, technical platform availability, and interpretation of the available evidence. Eastern and Western approaches increasingly share the principle that systemic therapy is the treatment backbone for advanced HCC with PVTT. The key clinical question is how interventional therapy should be integrated for selected patients rather than whether it should replace systemic therapy. Optimal management should be individualized through multidisciplinary decision-making based on PVTT extent, portal venous flow, liver function, intrahepatic and extrahepatic tumor burden, treatment goals, and institutional expertise. Future studies should standardize reporting of PVTT classification, portal vein patency, collateral circulation, liver reserve, tumor distribution, systemic therapy context, and treatment sequencing.

title: Selective endovascular aortic repair in connective tissue disease patients within a multidisciplinary program achieves comparable outcomes in high-risk patients.
abstract: BACKGROUND/OBJECTIVE: Endovascular aortic repair (ENDO) in patients with connective tissue disease (CTD) has historically been discouraged in society guidelines because of durability concerns. However, high-volume aortic centers increasingly employ ENDO strategies in carefully selected high-risk patients across scenarios such as rupture, dissection-related pathology, or hostile anatomy. Herein, we describe temporal ENDO adoption at our multidisciplinary CTD aortic program. METHODS: In this study, 92 patients with CTD undergoing aortic intervention at a single high-volume aortic center between 2005 and 2023 were analyzed. Patients were stratified by ENDO (n = 50) vs open repair (OPEN; n = 42). The primary outcome was freedom from aortic-related mortality (ARM). The secondary outcomes included technical success, complications, secondary aortic intervention (SAI), and overall survival. A prespecified contemporary analysis (2018-2023) was conducted to evaluate the outcomes following the establishment of a multidisciplinary CTD aortic program. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate survival and freedom from SAI. RESULTS: The mean age was 48 ± 16 years, and 34% (n = 31) were female. Diagnoses included Marfan syndrome (69%), Loeys-Dietz syndrome (15%), familial aortopathy (11%), and vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome (5%). Patients who underwent ENDO more frequently had prior sternotomy/open cardiac surgery (68% vs 19%; P < .0001), prior aortic surgery (70% vs 33%; P = .0007), and urgent presentation (50% vs 14%; P = .0004). Overall, 60% of these patients were deemed unfit for open repair by the multidisciplinary aortic team because of physiologic risk, anatomic complexity, or urgent presentation. The technical success rate was lower after ENDO (82% vs 98%; P = .02), and the 30-day reintervention rate was higher (16% vs 0%; P = .01). The median follow-up period was 2.3 years [interquartile range, 1.1-4.7]. SAIs occurred more frequently following ENDO (56% vs 12%; P = .0001), including planned staged procedures (ENDO: 28.6% vs OPEN: 20%; P = 1) and unplanned reinterventions (ENDO: 71.4% vs OPEN: 80%; P = 1). In the full cohort, patients undergoing ENDO had lower 3-year survival rates (71% ± 7% vs 92% ± 4%; log-rank P = .03). In the contemporary cohort, survival at 2 years following ENDO (n = 17) was poorer than that after OPEN (n = 42), although the difference did not reach significance (71% ± 14% vs 92% ± 4%; log-rank P = .1). Similarly, the rate of freedom from ARM was lower, but not significantly different (88% ± 12% vs 98% ± 2%; log-rank P = .4). CONCLUSIONS: Open repair remains the gold standard for connective tissue disease-associated aortic disease. In carefully selected high-risk patients, ENDO serves as a complementary strategy with acceptable contemporary survival and comparable freedom from ARM. Higher secondary intervention rates reflect both planned staged repair and unplanned surveillance-detected failure modes, underscoring the need for lifelong follow-up within multidisciplinary programs.

However, high-volume aortic centers increasingly employ ENDO strategies in carefully selected high-risk patients across scenarios such as rupture, dissection-related pathology, or hostile anatomy. Herein, we describe temporal ENDO adoption at our multidisciplinary CTD aortic program.

title: Impact of Undertreated Antithrombotic Therapy on Adverse Patient Outcomes: A Scientific Statement From the American Heart Association.
abstract: Antithrombotic therapy undertreatment includes omission, nonadherence, underdosing, and clinical circumstances that result in subtherapeutic antithrombotic levels. Antithrombotic undertreatment has profound implications for patient safety, public health, and healthcare costs. Due to deviation from evidence-based clinical practice, misperceptions of bleeding versus thrombotic risk, and inequities in healthcare access, many patients with atrial fibrillation, venous thromboembolism, or peripheral artery disease remain untreated or receive suboptimal anticoagulant dosing. Antithrombotic undertreatment has been shown to increase rates of ischemic stroke, systemic embolism, recurrent thrombosis, and mortality. Real-world data continue to highlight substantial gaps in care, which appear to be magnified in patients with inequity in social determinants of health. The emergence of antithrombotic stewardship, in concert with growing bodies of literature on antithrombotic agent underdosing, represents a transformative opportunity to address these gaps through structured, interprofessional, and evidence-based approaches. Through interdisciplinary collaboration, healthcare professionals are well positioned to enhance patient health and safety by recognizing and recommitting to reducing antithrombotic undertreatment.

title: [Lower-body Malperfusion Following Surgery for Stanford Type A Acute Aortic Dissection:Report of a Case].
abstract: The patient was an octogenarian woman who presented with sudden-onset chest pain and was diagnosed with Stanford type A acute aortic dissection. She underwent an emergency Bentall procedure with ascending aortic replacement. On postoperative day three, she developed rapid deterioration of renal function and bilateral lower-limb ischemia. Contrast-enhanced computed tomography (CT) revealed severe narrowing of the true lumen of the thoracic aorta, which caused malperfusion of the lower body. An entry was identified in the right common carotid artery (RCCA), and a stent-graft was deployed to close the entry;however, lower-limb perfusion did not improve sufficiently. Therefore, left axillo-bilateral femoral (or external iliac) artery bypass (axillo-bifemoral bypass) was subsequently performed. After the bypass procedure, expansion of the aortic true lumen and improvement in organ perfusion were obtained. To treat postoperative malperfusion following surgery for acute aortic dissection, closure of a branch entry alone may be insufficient, and extra-anatomic bypass can be a reliable option.

title: [Left Ventricular Mural Thrombus at the Suture Site After Left Ventricular Thrombectomy:Report of a Case].
abstract: A 45-year-old woman was diagnosed with myotonic dystrophy 17 years previously. Six days previously, she was referred to our hospital because of a tibial fracture from a fall injury. Echocardiography showed two thrombi in the left ventricular apex. Thrombectomy surgery was indicated because the thrombi were large and mobile. Cardiopulmonary bypass was initiated in the patient. A small, longitudinal incision was made on the left side of the left anterior descending artery under cardiac arrest to remove the thrombi. Two large thrombi were found at preoperative imaging. There were no intraoperative complications. Computed tomography (CT) showed a mural thrombus at the suture site on postoperative day 14. Anticoagulation therapy with warfarin was initiated. A follow-up echocardiography performed on postoperative day 22 showed marked improvement in apical akinesia. No thrombus was visualized in the left ventricle. A CT scan showed no thrombus on postoperative day 40.

title: [Bypass Grafting Using a Side Branch of the Aortic Arch Graft for Visceral Malperfusion Associated with Stanford Type A Acute Aortic Dissection].
abstract: Stanford type A acute aortic dissection complicated by abdominal organ malperfusion presents significant therapeutic challenges. We report the case of a 54-year-old man with aortic dissection extending from the ascending aorta to both external iliac arteries, with superior mesenteric artery (SMA) occlusion. Emergency exploratory laparotomy revealed non-necrotic but discolored bowel. An 8-mm ringed graft was anastomosed to the SMA and perfused via a temporary shunt from the right femoral artery. After color improvement, central aortic repair was performed under cardiopulmonary bypass. Perfusion to the SMA graft was integrated into the bypass circuit, and total arch replacement using a fourbranched graft was completed, with a branch anastomosed to the SMA graft. The patient recovered well postoperatively with conservative management. This technique enables early visceral reperfusion, ensures reliable inflow to the SMA, and avoids extensive vascular dissection. This surgical strategy may be a valuable option in similar complex cases.

We report the case of a 54-year-old man with aortic dissection extending from the ascending aorta to both external iliac arteries, with superior mesenteric artery (SMA) occlusion. Emergency exploratory laparotomy revealed non-necrotic but discolored bowel.

title: [The blue and painful leg - a case report of a syndrome and a vascular emergency].
abstract: May-Thurner syndrome is an entity associated with deep vein thrombosis of the lower extremity, in which an anatomical compression of the iliac veins leads to an increased risk of thrombosis. The syndrome stands close to the Phlegmasia cerulea dolens (PCD) - a seldom, severe form of deep vein thrombosis, in which near-complete venous outflow obstruction leads to critically reduced arterial perfusion of the extremity.

title: [A CASE OF MALIGNANT URETERAL LYMPHOMA DISTINGUISHED FROM URETERAL CARCINOMA THROUGH URETEROSCOPIC BIOPSY].
abstract: An 82-year-old male was referred to our department following the incidental detection of a mass in the left upper ureter on a computed tomography (CT) scan performed for abdominal aortic aneurysm follow-up. The imaging also revealed associated left hydronephrosis with ureteral dilatation, enlarged para-aortic lymph nodes, and a right pleural effusion. Although ureteral carcinoma was initially suspected, cytologic analysis of the pleural effusion and flow cytometry confirmed a diagnosis of malignant lymphoma. A ureteroscopic biopsy performed to further differentiate the ureteral lesion established the definitive diagnosis of primary ureteral malignant lymphoma. Following the administration of chemotherapy, the patient has remained in remission for one year with no evidence of recurrence.

title: Artificial intelligence for the detection of large vessel occlusion stroke and workflow optimization: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: To evaluate the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) tools on workflow efficiency, treatment times, and clinical outcomes in patients with large vessel occlusion (LVO) stroke. METHODS: We included observational studies that assessed the implementation of AI-based tools in the management of patients with suspected or confirmed LVO stroke. Eligible studies reported workflow, treatment, safety, or functional outcomes. Data were extracted on thrombolysis rates, CTA-to-arterial puncture time, door-to-puncture time, endovascular treatment (EVT) access, reperfusion success, symptomatic intracerebral hemorrhage (sICH), mortality, and functional independence (mRS 0-2) at 90 days. Random-effects models were applied to calculate pooled mean differences (MD) or risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs). RESULTS: Thirteen studies were included. AI implementation significantly reduced workflow delays: CTA-to-puncture time decreased by -40.20 minutes (95% CI -66.41 to -13.99; P<0.01) and door-to-puncture time by -23.17 minutes (95% CI -38.71 to -7.63; P<0.01). Thrombolysis administration showed no difference (RR 0.79; 95% CI 0.57-1.09; P=0.15). Similarly, no significant effects were observed for EVT access (RR 0.97; 95% CI 0.66-1.44; P=0.89), reperfusion success (RR 1.06; 95% CI 1.00-1.12; P=0.06), sICH (RR 0.63; 95% CI 0.30-1.35; P=0.23), or mortality (RR 0.72; 95% CI 0.38-1.37; P=0.32). However, AI-based workflows significantly improved functional independence at 90 days (RR 1.55; 95% CI 1.12-2.15; P=0.008). CONCLUSIONS: AI tools significantly improve treatment times and functional independence in acute LVO stroke without increasing adverse events.

title: Long-Term Complications and Secondary Procedures After Open Reduction and Internal Fixation of Ankle Fractures: A Descriptive Epidemiologic Study of Over 50,000 Patients.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Ankle fractures account for ~10% of fractures, ~40% treated operatively, yet absolute long-horizon complication and secondary-procedure estimates by fracture pattern and comorbidity remain limited. Prior series generally left decedents in the denominator as though still at risk. METHODS: Retrospective cohort study of aggregated, de-identified TriNetX data. Adults (≥18 years) undergoing operative ankle fracture fixation (2000-2015) were assigned to four fracture-pattern cohorts (isolated lateral, medial, bimalleolar, trimalleolar) and described across five overlapping comorbidity strata (diabetes, peripheral vascular disease, liver disease, renal failure, open fracture) plus a no-comorbidity reference. Aalen-Johansen cumulative incidence, with death as the competing event, was estimated for 90-day infection, venous thromboembolism (VTE), and mortality, and for nonunion/malunion repair, clinically attended arthritis, conversion to arthrodesis/arthroplasty, and hardware removal at 2, 5, and 10 years. No hypothesis was tested or comparison performed. RESULTS: Of 68,992 eligible adults, 56,724 carried no qualifying comorbidity codes (lateral 18,871; bimalleolar 16,794; trimalleolar 13,058; medial 8,001); 12,268 carried ≥1. In reference cohorts, 90-day cumulative incidence was 1.93-2.28% (infection), 1.61-2.19% (VTE), and 0.30-0.75% (mortality); comorbidity-stratum maxima were 9.61%, 8.62%, and 4.15%. At 10 years, reference-cohort cumulative incidence was 17.10-20.20% (clinically attended arthritis), 11.69-14.32% (hardware removal), 0.32-1.73% (nonunion/malunion repair), and 0.48-1.62% (arthrodesis/arthroplasty conversion), reaching 22.60% and 6.34% in comorbidity strata. Cumulative deaths by 10 years reached 29.2% (trimalleolar renal-failure stratum) versus 2.8-4.7% in the reference cohorts. CONCLUSION: Competing-risks cumulative incidence of coded complications and secondary procedures after ankle ORIF is reported by fracture pattern and comorbidity stratum. These unadjusted estimates support no comparison between patterns or strata but provide reference figures for preoperative counseling and for designing adjusted patient-level studies. # Level of Evidence IV, retrospective descriptive epidemiologic study. Keywords: ankle fracture; open reduction internal fixation; competing risks; cumulative incidence; clinically attended post-traumatic arthritis; administrative database.

title: Ovarian Vein Thrombosis: Diagnosis and Management of an Unusual-Site Venous Thrombosis for the Acute Physician.
abstract: Ovarian vein thrombosis (OVT) is a rare and under-recognised form of venous thromboembolism that is frequently missed due to absent or non-specific symptoms. Consequently, diagnosis is often delayed or made incidentally on cross-sectional imaging. Although OVT is usually associated with the postpartum period, it is increasingly recognised in patients with malignancy, pelvic surgery, and intra-abdominal infection. Potential complications may be life-threatening and include thrombus extension, pulmonary embolism, and, less commonly, sepsis and bleeding. Despite increasing recognition, evidence remains limited to small case series and reports. As such, there remains uncertainty regarding the optimal diagnostic approach and the use of anticoagulation, including indications for anticoagulation, duration of treatment, and follow-up. This review summarises the current evidence on the epidemiology, risk factors, clinical presentation, investigations, and management of OVT, and proposes a practical approach to the diagnosis and treatment of OVT for the acute physician.

title: Endoluminal Reconstruction of Complex Cervical Internal Carotid Artery Dissections Using the Surpass Elite Flow Diverter: A Technical Report.
abstract: Most cervical internal carotid artery (ICA) dissections heal with antithrombotic therapy. Complex lesions with flow-limiting stenosis, multisegment involvement, or persistent wide-necked pseudoaneurysms may fail medical management and require endovascular reconstruction, the indications for which remain individualized. Conventional carotid stents conform poorly to acute curves. Flow diverters reconstruct the parent lumen and accommodate angulation, but cervical use is off-label and experience with current-generation devices is limited. To our knowledge, we report the first use of the Surpass Elite flow diverter (Stryker Neurovascular, Fremont, CA) for cervical ICA dissection, in two patients, as the primary scaffold within hybrid constructs supported by coil embolization, angioplasty, and carotid stenting. An 18-year-old female with a Biffl grade III blunt injury had a right cervical dissection with critical narrowing of the true lumen and two large wide-necked pseudoaneurysms persisting despite antiplatelet therapy; coil embolization of both sacs, a single flow diverter, angioplasty, and telescoped carotid stents restored luminal caliber, with six-month angiography showing complete resolution without coil compaction. A 72-year-old male with a prior left middle cerebral artery infarct had a 6-cm chronic dissection of the cervical left ICA with dense distal calcification, aneurysmal dilatation, 70% stenosis, and angiographic hypoperfusion; two telescoped flow diverters and a carotid stent reconstructed the lumen without residual stenosis. Both patients received dual antiplatelet therapy starting seven days preoperatively, with P2Y12 reaction units verified within the target range, and neither had periprocedural complications. Reconstruction with the Surpass Elite within a hybrid construct was technically feasible in these two contrasting morphologies; two cases cannot establish efficacy, and the independent contribution of the device cannot be determined.

Complex lesions with flow-limiting stenosis, multisegment involvement, or persistent wide-necked pseudoaneurysms may fail medical management and require endovascular reconstruction, the indications for which remain individualized. Conventional carotid stents conform poorly to acute curves.

title: Severe Rhabdomyolysis With Minimal Muscular Symptoms After Long-Term Rosuvastatin Use: A Case Report and Brief Literature Review.
abstract: Severe rhabdomyolysis may present with limited muscular symptoms despite substantial biochemical injury. We describe a case of suspected statin-associated rhabdomyolysis during prolonged rosuvastatin exposure. A 65-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, peripheral arterial disease requiring bilateral below-knee amputations, and previous rhabdomyolysis presented with generalized weakness, abdominal discomfort, and left flank pain. He had taken rosuvastatin for more than 10 years. Admission investigations demonstrated creatine kinase of 23,107 U/L, creatinine of 7.80 mg/dL, markedly elevated aminotransferases, and brown urine. Creatine kinase subsequently peaked at 38,747 U/L despite limited muscular complaints. Progressive azotemia and encephalopathy prompted hemodialysis. Rosuvastatin was discontinued, and supportive treatment was provided without immunosuppression. The reported myositis panel was negative, while magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) demonstrated mild, nonspecific muscle edema. By discharge, weakness and encephalopathy had resolved, strength was preserved on focused examination, and creatine kinase had decreased to 1,003 U/L. The patient was advised to avoid all statins. Outpatient hemodialysis, rheumatology follow-up, and serial creatine kinase measurements were arranged, with anti-3-hydroxy-3-methylglutaryl-coenzyme A reductase (anti-HMGCR) antibody testing and muscle biopsy planned if creatine kinase remained persistently elevated after discharge. This case highlights the discrepancy between biochemical severity and muscular symptoms during long-standing statin exposure. Improvement after statin withdrawal and supportive care supported a suspected statin-associated process but did not establish causality or exclude an autoimmune mechanism. Continued clinical and biochemical follow-up was essential to document recovery and determine the need for further investigation.
englishSummary: Severe rhabdomyolysis may present with limited muscular symptoms despite substantial biochemical injury. We describe a case of suspected statin-associated rhabdomyolysis during prolonged rosuvastatin exposure. A 65-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease, poorly controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus, peripheral arterial disease requiring bilateral below-knee amputations, and previous rhabdomyolysis presented with generalized weakness, abdominal discomfort, and left flank pain.

title: Catastrophic High-Risk Pulmonary Embolism With Recurrent Cardiac Arrest Successfully Treated With Rescue Mechanical Thrombectomy After Systemic Thrombolysis.
abstract: High-risk pulmonary embolism (PE) complicated by cardiac arrest carries an extremely high mortality, and the optimal rescue strategy after an inadequate response to systemic thrombolysis remains uncertain. We report the case of a 53-year-old woman with previous deep-vein thrombosis who was admitted after an out-of-hospital cardiac arrest and subsequently experienced three additional episodes of cardiac arrest with pulseless electrical activity. Computed tomography pulmonary angiography demonstrated extensive bilateral central PE with severe right ventricular dilation and interventricular septal shift. Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase was administered. Despite thrombolysis and vasopressor/inotropic support, persistent cardiogenic-obstructive shock, electrical instability, and severe right ventricular pressure overload remained. Approximately 4 h after thrombolysis, rescue mechanical aspiration thrombectomy was performed using the Indigo® Aspiration System with Lightning Flash™ (Penumbra, Inc., Alameda, CA, USA). Ultrasound-guided right common femoral venous access was obtained with an 18 F sheath, and aspiration was performed in both pulmonary arteries. Pulmonary artery pressure decreased from 34 mmHg before aspiration to 25 mmHg at the end of the procedure. The patient subsequently achieved progressive hemodynamic stabilization. After prolonged mechanical ventilation and tracheostomy, neurological recovery was favorable. At discharge, echocardiography showed normal biventricular systolic function. This case illustrates that prompt escalation to rescue mechanical thrombectomy may be considered in selected patients with high-risk PE when shock, electrical instability, and right ventricular overload persist despite systemic thrombolysis.

title: A single-cell census of pulmonary endarterectomies tissue across different anatomical regions in chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA) remains one of potentially curative options for chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (CTEPH). The operation can remove proximal thromboembolic materials and their secondary branches. However, the cellular landscape and pathological features across different anatomical regions remain limited understood. METHODS: Ten patients with CTEPH undergoing PEA surgery and six reference distal pulmonary arteries were conducted single-cell transcriptomics to profile the cellular composition of the main and its bifurcate portion. RESULTS: Pronounced muscularised and fibrotic thrombi organisation were presented in the main portion, and the proportion of mononuclear phagocytes was significantly increased. Inflammatory response and pro-inflammatory activity were attributed to CD8+ effector T cells and nature killer cells subsets and a M1-like (high IL1B and TNF, minimal IL6) phenotypic macrophage subcluster. The colander-like lesions were dominant in the bifurcate portion, and the percentage of plasma cells was markedly increased. Immune dysregulation was induced from CD4 naïve T cells, and a downregulation of M2-like macrophage infiltration into the vascular wall. The expression of plasminogen activator, urokinase receptor, urokinase receptor (PLAUR; plasminogen activator) were observed in M2-like (high MRC1 and CD163, virtually no IL1B or TNF) macrophage in bifurcate portion. Notably, one of smooth muscle cells (SMCs) subclusters in the bifurcate portion gained more significantly myofibroblast markers than those in the main portion, and other subclusters remained the function of SMCs. CONCLUSIONS: The regions with colander-like lesions changes had more obviously T cell and macrophages driving immune-inflammatory response and SMCs differentiation, suggesting that combining therapeutic interventions after surgical removal of accessible thrombus may be beneficial. KEY POINTS: This study reveals the comprehensive cellular composition in main/lobar and bifurcate pulmonary endarterectomy (PEA) specimens at the single-cell level. The bifurcate regions with colander had more obviously T cell and macrophages driving immune-inflammatory response and smooth muscle cells (SMCs) differentiation, however, the remodelling of distal or micro-vessels still remained.

The operation can remove proximal thromboembolic materials and their secondary branches. title: Incremental prognostic and risk-stratification value of ultrasound-based Carotid Plaque Reporting and Data System (Plaque-RADS) classification for recurrent ischemic stroke in patients with low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis.
abstract: BACKGROUND: The Carotid Plaque Reporting and Data System (Plaque-RADS) is a system for stroke risk assessment. However, the clinical utility of ultrasound (US)-based Plaque-RADS remains unclear. This study aimed to assess the incremental prognostic value and risk stratification utility of US-based Plaque-RADS in patients with prior stroke and low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis. METHODS: Between January 2020 and December 2022, 231 patients with carotid plaque ipsilateral to the prior stroke and low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis were retrospectively screened, of whom 158 were included in the final analysis. US-based Plaque-RADS classification was assigned based on duplex US assessment of plaque features. Cox regression and subgroup analyses were performed to evaluate the association between high-risk US-based Plaque-RADS categories and recurrent ischemic stroke. Model discrimination was assessed using receiver operating characteristic curves and area under the curve (AUC), and clinical utility was evaluated using decision curve analysis. The association between increasing US-based Plaque-RADS categories and the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke was assessed by trend analysis. The incremental risk-stratification value of refined high-risk Plaque-RADS thresholds was quantified with net reclassification improvement (NRI) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI). Internal validation was performed using bootstrap resampling. RESULTS: vs. During the 3-year follow-up period, recurrent ischemic stroke occurred in 33 patients. High-risk US-based Plaque-RADS categories were significantly associated with recurrent ischemic stroke in patients with prior stroke and low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis, after adjusting for smoking, homocysteine, and intraplaque neovascularization [adjusted hazard ratio: 3.56; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.07-11.83, P=0.038]. No statistically significant interactions were observed across the subgroups (all P for interaction >0.05). The Plaque-RADS ≥3 model demonstrated a higher AUC than the conventional US model [0.816 (95% CI: 0.731-0.901)0.810 (95% CI: 0.720-0.899)] and provided a slight net benefit across selected threshold probabilities. Additionally, the risk of recurrent ischemic stroke increased with higher Plaque-RADS categories (P for trend <0.001). Among the models using different high-risk Plaque-RADS thresholds, the Plaque-RADS ≥3b model showed the best predictive performance (0.865, 95% CI: 0.799-0.930), compared with the Plaque-RADS ≥3 model and the Plaque-RADS ≥3c model [0.824 (95% CI: 0.740-0.906)]. The Plaque-RADS ≥3b model also showed moderate improvements in NRI [0.250; (95% CI: 0.088-0.557), P=0.017] and IDI [0.090; (95% CI: 0.000-0.185), P=0.049], compared with the Plaque-RADS ≥3 model. Bootstrap internal validation indicated limited optimism across all models. CONCLUSIONS: In patients with prior stroke and low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis, high-risk US-based Plaque-RADS categories were significantly associated with recurrent ischemic stroke. The US-based Plaque-RADS may help identify plaque phenotypes associated with an increased risk of recurrent ipsilateral ischemic stroke, while refined high-risk thresholds, particularly Plaque-RADS ≥3b, may provide additional value for risk stratification.

However, the clinical utility of ultrasound (US)-based Plaque-RADS remains unclear. This study aimed to assess the incremental prognostic value and risk stratification utility of US-based Plaque-RADS in patients with prior stroke and low-to-moderate-grade carotid stenosis.

title: Time-zero multimodal risk stratification for in-hospital mortality in acute aortic dissection: two-centre development, temporal and external validation, and occult shock phenotyping.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Acute aortic dissection (AAD) requires rapid anatomical diagnosis and early risk stratification, yet initial blood pressure alone may miss patients with concealed hypoperfusion. Although computed tomography angiography (CTA) defines dissection anatomy and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) provides bedside haemodynamic information, the incremental prognostic value of early TTE and the significance of normotensive hyperlactatemia remain uncertain. We aimed to develop and validate an initial 2-hour multimodal model integrating clinical, CTA, and TTE data to predict in-hospital mortality and to describe occult shock in normotensive AAD patients. METHODS: This retrospective two-centre cohort study included 2,584 adults with first-time AAD who completed CTA and TTE during the initial 2-hour assessment after emergency department triage. Cohorts were development (n=1,678; 2007-2017), internal temporal validation (n=452; 2018-2021), and external geographic/later-era validation (n=454; 2022-March 2024). Candidate variables were restricted to information available during this initial assessment window. Four supervised algorithms were compared, with ablation analyses assessing modality-specific contribution. RESULTS: XGBoost achieved optimism-corrected development area under the curve (AUC) of 0.86 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.82-0.88], internal validation 0.83 (0.79-0.87), and external validation 0.78 (0.74-0.82). Adding TTE to Clinical + CTA improved discrimination (Delta AUC +0.04, P=0.002) and integrated discrimination improvement (IDI) (+0.021, P=0.01). Normotensive occult shock occurred in 548/2,082 patients (26.3%) and was associated with mortality 15.9% versus 6.7% in metabolically stable normotension. CONCLUSIONS: In high-volume aortic centres where CTA and early TTE are routinely available, this initial 2-hour multimodal model showed temporal validation and moderate external discrimination for in-hospital mortality. TTE added prognostic information, particularly for type A disease, and normotensive hyperlactatemia identified a higher-risk subgroup; however, general use, type B performance, local recalibration, and action thresholds require prospective multicentre validation before clinical implementation.

Although computed tomography angiography (CTA) defines dissection anatomy and transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) provides bedside haemodynamic information, the incremental prognostic value of early TTE and the significance of normotensive hyperlactatemia remain uncertain. We aimed to develop and validate an initial 2-hour multimodal model integrating clinical, CTA, and TTE data to predict in-hospital mortality and to describe occult shock in normotensive AAD patients.

title: Signal of venous thromboembolism with ethinyl estradiol vs natural estrogens in oral contraceptives: analysis of the EudraVigilance and Food and Drug Administration Adverse Events Reporting System databases.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Disproportionality analyses in the Food and Drug Administration Adverse Events Reporting System (FAERS) and EudraVigilance reported lower reporting of venous thromboembolism (VTE) with natural estrogen-based combined oral contraceptives (COCs) than with ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel. However, using ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel as the reference showed reduced reporting only for natural estrogen-based products. We therefore reanalyzed both databases separately, using natural estrogen-based COCs as the reference. METHODS: 2 Previously extracted individual case safety report datasets and published disproportionality analyses were re-examined, using natural estrogen-based contraceptives as the comparator. Proportional reporting ratios (PRRs) were recalculated separately for each database. COCs were categorized as ethinylestradiol-based or natural estrogen-based formulations. Drospirenone-only pills were included for comparison. Analyses used pooled natural estrogen contraceptives, estetrol/drospirenone, or estradiol/dienogest as reference groups. Disproportionality was defined as PRR >2, at least 3 cases, and χ≥ 4. DISCUSSION: Consistent patterns were observed in EudraVigilance and FAERS. Compared with natural estrogen-based COCs, ethinylestradiol-based COCs showed a disproportionate reporting of VTE (EudraVigilance: PRR, 5.10 [95% CI, 4.68-5.56]; FAERS: PRR, 4.21 [95% CI, 3.49-5.08]). In EudraVigilance, when using estetrol/drospirenone as the reference, all ethinylestradiol-based formulations showed disproportionality according to the conventional PRR threshold. A similar trend was noted in FAERS, though not statistically significant, with the drospirenone-only formulation comparable to estetrol/drospirenone. CONCLUSION: This analysis revealed a consistent and disproportionate reporting of VTE associated with ethinylestradiol-based COCs compared with natural estrogen-based alternatives across 2 pharmacovigilance databases. These results, together with prior biological and observational research, support further reevaluation of COC options given the estrogenic component's potential influence on VTE risk.

However, using ethinylestradiol/levonorgestrel as the reference showed reduced reporting only for natural estrogen-based products. We therefore reanalyzed both databases separately, using natural estrogen-based COCs as the reference.

title: Impact of different follow-up methods on prognosis of diabetic foot patients after endovascular treatment: a multicenter retrospective cohort study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Diabetic foot ulcer (DFU) is a severe complication of diabetes mellitus, and endovascular treatment (EVT) has become the primary revascularization strategy. However, the impact of different post-procedure follow-up methods on clinical outcomes remains unclear. This study aimed to compare the effects of seven different follow-up approaches on prognosis in DFU patients after EVT. METHODS: This multicenter retrospective cohort study was conducted at three tertiary hospitals in China between June 2022 and June 2025. A total of 868 DFU patients who underwent successful EVT were enrolled and categorized into seven groups based on their primary follow-up method. The primary outcomes were 12-month wound healing rate and amputation-free survival (AFS). Secondary outcomes included major adverse limb events (MALE), reintervention rate, patient satisfaction, and glycemic control. Multivariable Cox regression and propensity score matching were used to adjust for confounders. RESULTS: Among 868 patients, the surgical hospital outpatient group demonstrated the highest 12-month wound healing rate (75.0%) and AFS rate (80.1%). The no follow-up group had the poorest outcomes (45.2% wound healing, 56.4% AFS). No follow-up was associated with significantly increased risk of MALE [adjusted hazard ratio (aHR) 2.15, 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.62-2.85]. WeChat follow-up (aHR 1.22, 95% CI: 0.88-1.69) showed non-significant differences compared with surgical hospital outpatient follow-up. CONCLUSIONS: Structured follow-up significantly improves wound healing and AFS in DFU patients after EVT. Digital health tools such as WeChat showed no statistically significant difference compared with traditional follow-up, but these observational data should not be interpreted as evidence of equivalent effectiveness. The absence of follow-up is associated with substantially worse outcomes. These findings are hypothesis-generating and warrant validation in prospective randomized trials.

However, the impact of different post-procedure follow-up methods on clinical outcomes remains unclear. This study aimed to compare the effects of seven different follow-up approaches on prognosis in DFU patients after EVT.

title: Libman-Sacks Endocarditis as the First Presentation of Systemic Lupus Erythematosus in a Young Man: A Multisystemic Diagnostic Challenge.
abstract: Systemic lupus erythematosus (SLE) is a complex, phenotypically varied disorder that possesses wide-ranging cardiac involvement. Libman-Sacks endocarditis (LSE) is one such cardiac manifestation, which results from the deposition of verrucous, sessile lesions favoring the left-sided heart valves. LSE is typically clinically silent without significant valvular dysfunction. Such patients with LSE, however, are those most susceptible to a more severe clinical phenotype resulting from SLE. Here, we report a unique case of a 22-year-old man initially presenting with unilateral leg swelling found to be secondary to a deep-vein thrombosis. He subsequently developed a constellation of acute symptoms, including embolic strokes, splenic infarction, proteinuric kidney injury, and significant mitral regurgitation, all of which mimicked bacterial endocarditis. His complex, multi-systemic disease course presented diagnostic challenges. We highlight the need in such complex cases for a specialist-led multidisciplinary approach, including cardiologists and rheumatologists, to guide serological and radiological investigations. Early use of echocardiography, in particular 3D transesophageal imaging, was paramount in clinching the diagnosis of LSE as an index presentation of SLE and in the transition from intravenous antibiotics to immunosuppression. Our case underscores the importance of the multidisciplinary team and the role of echocardiography in identifying such patients with LSE in SLE and thereby those most vulnerable to significant end-organ sequelae.

title: When Diabetes Mimics Scleroderma: Cheiroarthropathy and Neuropathic Digital Erosions in Type 2 Diabetes.
abstract: Diabetic cheiroarthropathy is an underrecognized complication of diabetes characterized by limited finger joint extension and thickened, waxy skin of the hands. It can clinically mimic several rheumatologic conditions, particularly systemic sclerosis, creating a diagnostic challenge. We report the case of a 68-year-old man with long-standing type 2 diabetes mellitus who presented with hand stiffness and contractures, scleroderma-like skin thickening, and nonpainful crusted digital erosions, raising concern for systemic sclerosis-associated digital ulceration. He underwent rheumatologic evaluation and received immunosuppressive therapy without improvement in the cutaneous findings, prompting further clinical reassessment. His overall clinical phenotype, including a positive prayer sign, skin thickening confined to the digits, absence of Raynaud phenomenon, normal nailfold capillaries, and negative anti-Scl-70 and anticentromere antibodies, favored diabetic cheiroarthropathy over systemic sclerosis. The digital erosions were considered likely multifactorial, with contributions from unrecognized trauma in the setting of diabetic neuropathy and possible vascular compromise related to peripheral arterial disease and tobacco use. This case highlights the clinical overlap between diabetic cheiroarthropathy and systemic sclerosis, particularly when digital erosions accompany scleroderma-like hand changes. Recognizing this presentation may help prevent misdiagnosis and unnecessary immunosuppression while directing management toward glycemic control, prevention of repetitive trauma, local wound care, and occupational therapy.

title: Short-Term Outcomes of Lower-Extremity Surgical Revascularization for Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia Among Yemeni Patients: A Prospective Observational Study.
abstract: BACKGROUND: Chronic limb-threatening ischemia (CLTI) carries a high risk of amputation and mortality. We evaluated short-term clinical, hemodynamic, and quality-of-life outcomes after open lower-extremity surgical revascularization in a Yemeni cohort. METHODS: This single-center prospective observational cohort study was conducted at Al-Thawra Modern General Hospital, Sana'a, Yemen. We enrolled 39 consecutive adults with CLTI (Rutherford categories 4-6) who were selected for and considered fit to undergo open lower-extremity surgical revascularization between December 2022 and September 2024; follow-up was completed in December 2024. The study protocol was reviewed and approved by the Al-Thawra Hospital Ethics Committee (approval no. 33-2026), and written informed consent was obtained from all participants. The study was not registered. This was an exploratory consecutive cohort; no formal sample-size calculation was performed, and no contemporaneous endovascular, nonoperative, or primary-amputation comparator group was included. Primary endpoints were graft patency and limb salvage at three months. Secondary outcomes were secondary patency, postoperative complications, and changes in ankle-brachial index (ABI) and Vascular Quality of Life Questionnaire-6 (VascuQoL-6) scores. Paired comparisons used Wilcoxon signed-rank tests; Fisher's exact tests were used for categorical comparisons. RESULTS: The mean age was 60.9 years (SD 9.7), and 30 patients (76.9%) were male. Diabetes mellitus and hypertension were present in 34 (87.2%) and 30 (76.9%) patients, respectively. Nineteen patients (48.7%) had ischemic rest pain, and 20 (51.3%) had tissue loss. Great saphenous vein (GSV) and polytetrafluoroethylene (PTFE) grafts were used in 28 (71.8%) and 11 (28.2%) patients, respectively. At three months, primary patency was 84.6% (33/39 grafts; 95% CI 70.3%-92.8%), secondary patency was 89.7% (35/39 grafts; 95% CI 76.4%-95.9%), and limb salvage was 89.7% (35/39 patients; 95% CI 76.4%-95.9%). Given the small cohort, the confidence intervals around these estimates were relatively wide. Among the 35 patients with limb preservation, mean ABI increased from 0.35 (SD 0.11) to 0.55 (SD 0.12; mean difference 0.21, 95% CI 0.19-0.23; p<0.001), and mean VascuQoL-6 score increased from 10.3 (SD 2.9) to 16.6 (SD 4.0; mean difference 6.3, 95% CI 5.6-7.1; p<0.001). Complications occurred in nine patients (23.1%). In an exploratory unadjusted subgroup analysis, GSV use was associated with higher primary patency than PTFE use (92.9% vs 63.6%, p=0.042). CONCLUSION: In this single-center prospective cohort, open surgical revascularization was feasible and was associated with 89.7% limb salvage and 84.6% primary patency at three months. Improvements in ABI and VascuQoL-6 were observed among patients with limb preservation. Autologous GSV use was associated with higher primary patency; this finding requires confirmation in larger, adjusted studies.
